methods: 3.1 Data sources, linkage and study populations

We conducted an ecological panel study of 204 countries and territories in seven Global Burden of Disease (GBD) super-regions, covering 2005–2023. We described the burden of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) and malaria, assessed spatial clustering and socioeconomic inequality, examined associations with external health financing, and modelled potential health losses under reductions in development assistance for health (DAH). The unit of analysis was the country-year; estimates therefore describe population-level associations rather than individual effects.^{27} Reporting followed the Guidelines for Accurate and Transparent Health Estimates Reporting (GATHER) and relevant STROBE recommendations.^{28,29} The GATHER checklist is provided in the appendix.

We linked five public sources: GBD 2023, World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI), World Health Organization (WHO) indicators disseminated through the UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) database, Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) Financing Global Health estimates, and Natural Earth boundaries.^{26,30–33} Records were harmonised using ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes, GBD location identifiers and the GBD super-region hierarchy. Table S1 summarises source coverage; Figure 1 shows the analytical workflow.

Descriptive analyses covered 204 GBD locations. Spatial analyses included 203 locations with Natural Earth polygons, excluding Tokelau. Financing analyses began with 168 locations outside the GBD high-income super-region; this geographical classification is not equivalent to World Bank low- and middle-income status. After covariate exclusions, the NTD panel included 153 locations. Malaria models additionally required a maximum age-standardised malaria DALY rate above 10 per 100 000 during 2005–2023: 78 locations met this threshold and 77 entered the complete-case panel. Inequality analyses required population data; the original Theil analysis also excluded zero-rate locations. Inequality time series used all 204 locations, weighted by GBD population for 1990 and by population implied by GBD all-age counts divided by crude rates for 2010 and 2023.

Countries were assigned to the 21 GBD regions using the GBD location hierarchy. Summed country DALY counts reproduced published regional totals to within 0.2% in 17 regions and within 1.5–4.2% in the Caribbean, Central Europe, Western Europe and Oceania, where GBD regional aggregates include locations without separate country estimates. In the linkage file, Finland carried the Natural Earth code for the Åland Islands (ALA); it was reassigned to Western Europe for regional analyses and to the Finland polygon for supplementary maps.

WHO-reported indicators provided outcomes not obtained from GBD: the number of people requiring NTD interventions (SDG 3.3.5) and malaria incidence per 1000 people at risk (SDG 3.3.3).^{31,34} These were retrieved through the UN SDG database. IHME Financing Global Health estimates for 1990–2030 were used to calibrate the funding-cut scenarios.^{26} Estimated DAH fell from US$49.6 billion in 2024 to a preliminary US$38.4 billion in 2025, approximately 22%. Spatial analyses used Natural Earth administrative level 0 polygons at 1:50 million scale.^{35} After projection to Robinson coordinates (ESRI:54030), the scripts generated an interior representative point for each country polygon. Euclidean distances between these points defined the original spatial weights. GBD extracts were retained as raw CSV and JSON files; WDI and SDG series were retrieved through public APIs. Truncated requests were split into shorter year windows, and country-year coverage was checked after assembly. The GBD outcome panel contained 3876 observations (204 locations × 19 years), with no missing outcomes. Raw data, processed datasets and scripts are archived with the paper. Natural Earth records with missing ISO codes were matched using administrative codes. The supplied WDI extract covered 2005–2024; the panel retained 2005–2023. Table S11 lists indicator codes, definitions, transformations and lags.
3.2 Burden outcomes

GBD 2023 supplied annual all-age DALY counts and age-standardised DALY rates for the combined NTD-and-malaria category and malaria during 2005–2023. NTD totals excluding malaria were obtained by subtraction. The 2023 cross-section additionally contained 19 individual NTD components, selected deaths and prevalence estimates, and published uncertainty intervals (UIs). The 19 component DALY counts reproduced the 2023 NTD total. Historical country-level extracts covered selected years, whereas super-regional trends extended from 1990 to 2023. Age-standardised rates were expressed per 100 000 population.^{30} Percentage changes and their UIs were imported from GBD rather than calculated from endpoint bounds.

For regional analyses we extracted, for each of the 21 GBD regions, 2023 all-age DALY counts with 95% UIs, all-age and age-standardised rates, and GBD-published percentage changes in age-standardised rates between 2010 and 2023, with UIs, for the NTD-and-malaria aggregate and for malaria. For the fatal and non-fatal composition, we extracted 2023 all-age YLDs and YLLs with UIs for each super-region and globally. NTD values excluding malaria were obtained by subtraction and carry no interval because GBD does not publish draws for that difference. Country-level age-standardised rates and counts for 1990 and 2010 supported the inequality time series and the national comparisons. GBD publishes country-level percentage changes with UIs only for the NTD-and-malaria aggregate; changes for NTDs excluding malaria and for malaria alone were computed from point estimates and are reported without intervals.
3.3 Financing exposures and covariates

The primary exposure was external health expenditure as a share of current health expenditure (CHE), scaled per 10 percentage points. The secondary exposure was log(1 + external health expenditure per capita). WDI health-financing series derive from the WHO Global Health Expenditure Database (GHED), which follows the System of Health Accounts 2011.^{32,33} External expenditure includes bilateral, multilateral and philanthropic financing originating outside the country. Both exposures were lagged by 2 years to allow for programme implementation and reduce contemporaneous feedback; lagging alone does not resolve endogeneity.^{14,36} Monetary values were expressed in current US dollars.

NTD rates were natural-log transformed; malaria rates used log (1 + rate) to accommodate values approaching zero. NTD and malaria models were fitted separately. Covariates were selected a priori from aid–health studies and the WHO NTD road map.^{12,14,34} Models adjusted for log domestic government health expenditure per capita (lagged 2 years), log LDI, UHC effective coverage per 10 points, and basic sanitation and drinking-water coverage per 10 percentage points.^{37} SDI was excluded from the primary models because it incorporates income; it was used for inequality ranking and sensitivity analyses. Collinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors on within-transformed covariates; maximum values were 6.1 for NTDs and 6.4 for malaria. These were interpreted as diagnostics rather than against an absolute threshold.^{38}
3.4 Missing data

GBD outcomes and the GBD covariates including Socio-demographic Index (SDI), universal health coverage (UHC) effective-coverage index and lag-distributed income per capita (LDI) were complete. Missingness affected WDI series. In the modelling frame of 2688 country-years (168 locations, 2007–2022), missing values accounted for 15.1% of lagged external expenditure share, 8.2% of lagged domestic government health expenditure, 4.7% of sanitation coverage and 4.3% of drinking-water coverage (Table S10a).

Fourteen locations had no usable lagged external expenditure share in the modelling window: American Samoa, Bermuda, Cook Islands, Guam, Montenegro, Northern Mariana Islands, Niue, Puerto Rico, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Slovakia, Tokelau, Türkiye, Taiwan and the US Virgin Islands. Nicaragua also lacked sanitation and drinking-water observations. These exclusions reduced the eligible NTD sample from 168 to 153 locations.

We assessed associations between incomplete records and log NTD DALY rate, SDI, year and super-region using logistic regression with country-clustered standard errors. These diagnostics described observed missingness patterns but could not establish whether data were missing at random.

Within each country, interior WDI gaps were linearly interpolated without a maximum gap length; final observations were carried forward for at most 2 years. We did not extrapolate backwards or impute outcomes. Remaining incomplete records were excluded from each model. We reconstructed a model-specific flag from the observed input series, using exposure values 2 years before the outcome and contemporaneous sanitation and drinking-water values. This identified filled model inputs in 62 of 2287 NTD observations (2.7%) and 14 of 1187 malaria observations (1.2%).

Missing-data sensitivity analyses used observed model inputs only, restricted the sample to countries with complete observations throughout 2007–2022, and used multiple imputation.^{39–43} Excluding observations with the corrected model-specific filling flag produced the same sample as requiring observed inputs, so these checks are not independent robustness tests. The original imputation model used four WDI variables, LDI, UHC, SDI, year, the observed outcome and country means of observed covariates. Outcomes were predictors only.

The multiple-imputation implementation used Bayesian ridge regression with posterior sampling, 15 iterations and 20 datasets. Missing country-level auxiliary means were replaced with the corresponding across-country median. It imposed no explicit bounds on percentage variables and recorded no convergence diagnostics. Estimates were pooled using Rubin’s rules.^{40} Because convergence diagnostics were not recorded, the multiple-imputation estimates in Table S10b are a secondary check on the complete-case and interpolation analyses rather than a primary result; the variance summary is the proportion of total variance attributable to the between-imputation component, not a finite-sample fraction-of-missing-information estimate.

Cross-sectional exposures used the latest available observation during 2019–2023. Complete records were available for 169 of 204 locations globally; 145 remained after excluding the GBD high-income super-region. Table S9 describes the global complete-case comparison. The WHO NTD intervention-need proportion divided the 2023 count by the latest available WDI population value, so its denominator was not necessarily from 2023.

Scenario analyses used 2022 population where 2023 values were unavailable. Missing GDP per capita for South Sudan, Yemen and Eritrea was replaced by the study-sample median for monetary valuation only, not for DALY projections.
3.5 Descriptive, regional and national analyses

We summarised 2023 all-age DALY counts, shares of global burden and age-standardised rates by super-region (Table 1), cause (Table S2), GBD region (Table S16) and country. Countries were ranked by age-standardised rate and by absolute count for NTDs excluding malaria and for malaria (Table S18), and for each of the 19 NTD causes we identified the country with the largest share of global DALYs, the three largest contributors and the country with the highest age-standardised rate (Table S20). Countries whose rates rose between 2010 and 2023 were identified in two ways: from GBD-published percentage changes with UIs for the NTD-and-malaria aggregate (classified as a significant increase or decrease when the UI excluded zero) and from point estimates for NTDs excluding malaria and for malaria, restricting malaria to countries with a 2010 rate above 1 per 100 000 (Table S19).
3.6 Socioeconomic inequality

We summarised 2023 all-age DALY counts, shares of global burden and age-standardised rates by super-region, and changes in age-standardised rates from 2010 to 2023 (Table 1). Cause-specific estimates are provided in Table S2. Maps, heat maps and trend plots describe geographical and temporal patterns (Figure 2, Figure 3 & Figure 4). Socioeconomic inequality was measured using a population-weighted concentration index, ranking countries from lowest to highest SDI in the same year (1990, 2010 and 2023).^{44–46} The index equals twice the weighted covariance of the age-standardised rate and fractional socioeconomic rank, divided by the weighted mean rate. Negative values indicate concentration in lower-SDI countries. We obtained 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from 2000 country-level bootstrap resamples using the percentile method.

Absolute inequality was measured with the slope index of inequality (SII). Countries were ordered by SDI and each was assigned the midpoint of its cumulative population share (its fractional rank, from 0 to 1). The SII is the slope of a population-weighted linear regression of the age-standardised rate on this rank, which estimates the difference in rate between the hypothetical highest-SDI and lowest-SDI ends of the distribution; negative values indicate higher rates in low-SDI countries. The relative SII divides the SII by the population-weighted mean rate.^{47} The concentration index, the SII and the relative SII were estimated for 1990, 2010 and 2023. CIs used 2000 bootstrap resamples of countries. Changes between years were estimated by resampling countries jointly across years (paired bootstrap), so that each replicate compares the same set of countries; a change was considered distinguishable from zero when its 95% CI excluded zero (Table S15a; Figure S1).

We calculated the population-weighted Theil T index and decomposed it into between-super-region and within-super-region components (Table 2; Figure 5).^{48,49} The original calculation required positive rates and available population, yielding 199 locations for NTDs and 86 for malaria. A sensitivity analysis retained zero malaria rates among all 199 locations with population data, assigning zero to the limiting term 0 log (0).

A nested Theil T decomposition used the GBD hierarchy to split total inequality into three additive parts: between the seven super-regions, between the 21 regions within super-regions, and between countries within regions. It was computed for 1990, 2010 and 2023 among countries with positive rates (Table S15b).
3.7 Spatial autocorrelation

Spatial dependence was assessed before regression modelling.^{50} We constructed row-standardised weights from the six nearest neighbours of each projected country representative point. This retained island states in the spatial analysis. Sensitivity analyses used four or eight neighbours and a 2500 km inverse-distance band (Table S7).^{50,51} Global Moran’s I assessed clustering in log (1 + age-standardised DALY rate), with 9999 permutations for inference.^{52} We reported permutation p values and z scores. Analyses were repeated within the sample outside the GBD high-income super-region and, for malaria, within endemic locations. Local Moran statistics identified high–high and low–low clusters and high–low or low–high outliers.^{53} Multiple testing across 203 locations was addressed using the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate procedure at q<0.05.^{54} Cluster maps are shown in Figure 5.

To assess persistence of clusters, global Moran’s I and local indicators were recomputed for 1990, 2010 and 2023 with the same weights and false-discovery-rate control, and countries entering or leaving high–high clusters between 2010 and 2023 were listed (Table S21; Figure S4).
3.8 Panel econometric models

The primary analysis used within-country variation to account for time-invariant country characteristics.^{55} Cross-sectional ordinary least squares (OLS) with super-region fixed effects and a maximum-likelihood spatial error model provided between-country comparisons.^{12,14,21} Cross-sectional models additionally adjusted for rural population share. NTD panel models included 153 countries and 2287 country-years during 2007–2022; malaria models included 77 countries and 1187 country-years. The preferred specification included country and year fixed effects, the 2-year-lagged financing exposure and the covariates listed above. We retained 2007–2022 as the original primary window and examined extension through 2023 in a post-review sensitivity analysis. Additional checks omitted UHC and excluded observations without matching UHC or LDI records in the supplied raw archive (Table S15). We compared pooled OLS, random effects, two-way fixed effects with country-clustered standard errors, correlated random effects (Mundlak), first differences, and fixed effects with country-specific linear trends.^{55–57} Mundlak models included country means of time-varying regressors. Country-specific trends were removed from outcomes and regressors before estimation. Each estimator was fitted using both financing exposures.

Diagnostics comprised the Breusch–Pagan test for country-level heterogeneity, Hausman and cluster-robust Mundlak tests, Pesaran’s test for cross-sectional dependence, the Wooldridge test for serial correlation, and a modified Wald test for groupwise heteroskedasticity (Table S3).^{56,58–62} The preferred two-way fixed-effects model used Driscoll–Kraay standard errors with a Bartlett kernel and bandwidth of 3 to address heteroskedasticity, serial correlation and cross-sectional dependence.^{63,64} Sensitivity analyses used bandwidths of 1, 2 and 4 and country-clustered standard errors. These checks assess inference sensitivity; they do not remove the limitations of a 16-year panel. For NTDs, coefficients and confidence limits were transformed as 100 × [exp(β) − 1] to express percentage differences in DALY rates. For malaria, this transformation applies to rate + 1 and approximates a percentage difference in the rate when rates are large relative to 1. For the per-capita exposure, multiplying the coefficient by log (2) estimates a doubling of expenditure plus US$1, not a doubling of expenditure itself. All coefficients were interpreted as conditional associations. Fixed effects do not remove time-varying confounding, and lagging does not establish causal identification.^{36,65} We assessed consistency across estimators rather than relying on statistical significance alone.

To present between-country and within-country associations side by side in the same sample, we fitted a correlated random-effects (Mundlak) model containing the time-varying exposure, its country mean, the five covariates and their country means, and year indicators, with country-clustered standard errors. The coefficient on the time-varying exposure is the within-country association; the sum of that coefficient and the coefficient on the country mean is the between-country association; the coefficient on the country mean tests whether the two differ (Table S23).^{56,57}

Because recent evaluations of development assistance report mortality, the preferred two-way fixed-effects model was re-estimated with the GBD 2023 age-standardised malaria death rate, on the log(1 + rate) scale, as outcome for the 77 malaria-endemic countries, with Driscoll–Kraay and country-clustered standard errors (Table S24).
3.9 Spatial panel models

Models used row-standardised six-nearest-neighbour weights and maximum likelihood with the Lee–Yu fixed-effects transformation.^{66} Year effects were removed by cross-country demeaning. Analyses were restricted to balanced 16-year panels of 130 countries for NTDs and 71 for malaria. The intended SAR summaries are direct, indirect and total associations derived from the spatial multiplier (I − ρW)⁻¹^{67} (Table S12).
3.10 Geographically weighted regression

GWR and MGWR examined the 2023 NTD association in 145 locations outside the GBD high-income super-region with complete inputs.^{68–70} Financing exposure was mean external expenditure share during 2019–2022. The log NTD DALY rate and all four predictors (external share, UHC, log LDI and sanitation coverage) were standardised to mean 0 and SD 1. Models used an adaptive bisquare kernel. Bandwidths were selected by minimising the corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc), using golden-section search for GWR and back-fitting for MGWR.^{71} MGWR estimated a separate bandwidth for each covariate. Local inference used the MGWR multiple-testing adjustment based on covariate-specific effective numbers of parameters.^{72} Fit was compared with global OLS using AICc and R² (Tables S6a–b; Figure 7C).
3.11 Predictive modelling

We compared elastic net, random forest and LightGBM for prediction of log NTD DALY rates during 2007–2023, using validation schemes that reflected the panel and spatial structure.^{73–78} Elastic-net penalty strength and mixing proportion (0.1, 0.5 or 0.9) were selected by internal five-fold cross-validation. Random forest used 500 trees, a minimum leaf size of 5 and 50% of features at each split. LightGBM used 600 trees, learning rate 0.03, 15 leaves, and row and column subsampling of 0.8. Tree-model hyperparameters were fixed before test-set evaluation. In the supplied elastic-net implementation, scaling preceded internal cross-validation and ordinary internal folds did not preserve the grouped or temporal validation structure. These results require rerunning with preprocessing and tuning inside structure-appropriate training folds. All models used 13 features: both financing exposures, the five panel covariates, rural population share, out-of-pocket expenditure share, SDI, year, and two projected coordinate variables. Validation comprised random five-fold splits, grouped five-fold splits by country, leave-one-super-region-out validation, and temporal validation (training: 2007–2017; testing: 2018–2023). Random splits were included to illustrate potentially optimistic performance when countries appear in both training and test sets. Temporal validation included a linear benchmark with country fixed effects and a linear time trend, allowing extrapolation beyond the training years. Test-period covariates were observed, so temporal results describe conditional predictions rather than fully prospective forecasts. Test samples differed between validation schemes and hyperparameters were tuned without a fully nested design, so comparisons are valid within, not across, validation schemes and are slightly optimistic for the tuned models. Performance was assessed on the log scale using root-mean-square error (RMSE), mean absolute error and R² (Table S5; Figure 7B). Mean absolute Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values summarised feature contributions to LightGBM predictions in the full dataset.^{79} These were interpreted as model attribution, not causal effects.
3.12 Scenario models of development-assistance cuts

We used two conditional scenarios for annual health losses under external-financing reductions. Neither identifies a causal effect. The scenarios reduced each country’s external expenditure by 5–15% (mild), 19–26% (reference) or 40–60% (severe). The reference range encompassed IHME’s estimated 22% decline in global DAH between 2024 and 2025; the severe scenario represented larger reductions.^{21,26} The same proportional cut was applied to 153 locations with financing data, using the latest available 2019–2023 financing baseline and 2023 burden and population.

The accounting model summed cause-specific changes in all-age DALYs per person between 2010 and 2023, truncated each country’s total gain at zero, and multiplied it by 2023 population, external expenditure share and the funding-cut proportion. This assumes that gains attributable to external financing equal its share of health spending and reverse proportionately after a cut. All 19 NTD causes, including other NTDs, yellow fever, Ebola, Guinea worm disease and Zika, had GBD 2023 baselines for 2010; the 2010 sum of the 19 causes was 21.76 million DALYs. The econometric model recalculated external expenditure share as s(1 − c)/(1 − sc), where s is the baseline share expressed as a fraction and c is the proportional cut. It multiplied the share change in units of 10 percentage points by the preferred panel coefficient and applied exp (βΔx) − 1 to baseline all-age DALYs. For NTDs, this additionally assumes that an age-standardised association transfers to all-age counts. For malaria, whose outcome is log(1 + rate), each draw computed the new value of (1 + age-standardised rate) by multiplying the baseline (1 + rate) by the exponentiated coefficient–exposure product, subtracted 1 to obtain the new rate, and applied the ratio of the new to the baseline rate to baseline all-age DALYs.

Uncertainty was propagated through 4000 Monte Carlo draws.^{80} We treated each published DALY point estimate as a log-normal median and set the log-scale standard deviation to [log(upper UI) − log(lower UI)]/3.92. Simulated draws were independent across countries and causes, with shared standard-normal draws between 2010 and 2023 in the primary analysis and independent year draws in sensitivity analysis. These are approximations from published summaries, not original GBD posterior draws, and generally do not reproduce both published bounds exactly. Each simulation sampled a funding cut uniformly within the scenario range and applied it to all countries. For the econometric model, coefficients were sampled from a normal distribution using the preferred estimate and Driscoll–Kraay standard error. Country estimates were summed within each draw to obtain super-regional and overall projections. We reported medians and 2.5th–97.5th percentiles; these intervals reflect the specified simulation assumptions. Projected DALYs were valued at one time each country’s GDP per capita in current US dollars, with 0.5 and 3 times GDP per capita examined in sensitivity analyses. These multiples provide an illustrative monetary valuation, not a cost-effectiveness threshold or an estimate of fiscal losses.^{81–83} The domestic financing gap was calculated at each scenario midpoint as external expenditure per capita × population × proportional cut, summed by super-region. This was expressed as a percentage of domestic government health expenditure to describe the increase needed to replace lost external funds (Table S14).
3.13 External triangulation with WHO surveillance series

GBD country estimates were compared with two WHO series obtained from the UN SDG database: the number of people requiring interventions against NTDs (SDG 3.3.5), expressed per 100 000 population, and malaria incidence per 1000 population at risk (SDG 3.3.3). Spearman rank correlations with GBD age-standardised DALY rates were computed for 2010 and 2023, for NTDs excluding malaria across all reporting countries and for malaria across endemic countries with non-zero values (Table S21). The comparison assesses agreement in the ordering of countries, not in absolute levels, because the measures differ in construct.
3.14 Sensitivity analyses

Sensitivity analyses examined alternative spatial weights and samples; financing exposure definitions; SDI substitution and WHO-reported outcomes; panel estimators and country trends; spatial models; missing-data strategies; and included versus excluded locations. Scenario analyses varied temporal dependence of burden draws, attribution of gains to external financing, and monetary valuation (Tables S7, S10b, S12 and S13). Additional analyses extended the panel to 2023, omitted UHC, excluded observations without matching UHC or income records and retained zero rates in the Theil decomposition (Table S22).
3.15 Statistical software and reproducibility

Analyses used Python: pandas and NumPy for data management; statsmodels and linearmodels for regression and diagnostics; PySAL packages for spatial analyses; scikit-learn for imputation, elastic net, random forest and validation; LightGBM and SHAP for predictive modelling; and GeoPandas and matplotlib for maps and figures.^{70,84} Code and the harmonised analytical dataset are in the study GitHub repository (https://github.com/VincentUwumboriyhieGmayinaam/NTD-Malaria-Burden-Financing). An AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) was used to write and run the analysis code under author supervision; the authors reviewed and verified the code and outputs. Random processes used fixed seeds (scenario seed: 20261007). Tests were two-sided at α=0.05, with emphasis on estimates and 95% CIs. Code, processed datasets and execution instructions are provided in the appendix. Revision analyses are in scripts step5_revisions.py (inequality over time, regions, YLD–YLL, national rankings, cause leaders, LISA over time, WHO triangulation), step5_theil_regions.py, step5_mundlak_between_within.py, step5_mortality_sensitivity.py and step3_scenarios_v2.py.

search: We searched PubMed from inception to Oct 21, 2026, without language restrictions, using six strings: (S1) NTD or malaria burden with Global Burden of Disease or DALYs; (S2) NTD or malaria with inequality, concentration index or slope index; (S3) NTD or malaria with spatial analysis, Moran’s I or hotspots; (S4) USAID, funding cuts or donor funding with NTDs, malaria or mortality, January 2024–October 2026; (S5) development assistance for health or official development assistance with NTD, malaria or child mortality; and (S6) domestic health financing, displacement or donor transition. The searches identified 767 records (S1 206; S2 29; S3 163; S4 99; S5 176; S6 94); after removal of 63 duplicates, 704 were unique and 698 could be retrieved and screened by title. We excluded 602 on title and 20 on abstract (commentaries without data, superseded analyses, out-of-scope designs), leaving 76 eligible studies. The 44 most relevant and recent, prioritised within five themes, are summarised in Table E1; two landmark national studies are flagged. WHO and IHME reports were reviewed for current indicator values. Supplementary targeted searches of Lancet journals for 2025–26 comment on the aid cuts identified commentaries and letters without primary data.
